description:
Somos un equipo de la Institución Educativa Gimnasio La Salada, ubicada en Segovia, Antioquia, Colombia. Nos apasiona la tecnología, la ciencia, la programación, la innovación y la exploración espacial. Creemos que las grandes ideas nacen de la creatividad, la curiosidad y el trabajo en equipo.

Nos interesa participar en NASA Space Apps Challenge porque queremos aprender, compartir conocimientos y desarrollar soluciones innovadoras a problemas reales de nuestro planeta y del universo.
summary:
"On the Trail of Planet X: The SPHEREx Sky in Motion" ("Tras la pista del Planeta X: el cielo de SPHEREx en movimiento") is a public, interactive, Spanish-language website that lets anyone explore the infrared sky observed by NASA's SPHEREx mission. Users can navigate a sky map, select a star and, using a time slider, see where it moves in the past or future, up to 20,000 years. The site also includes official SPHEREx images, fact cards on celestial objects, a space assistant, and an educational section on the search for Planet X.

It addresses the "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge by showing how the sky changes over time, using the same method astronomers rely on: comparing positions on different dates to detect moving objects.

It matters because SPHEREx produces more data than any single person could ever review. A free, simple tool in our own language brings students and citizens across Latin America closer to real NASA data and invites them to take part in science.
details:
On the Trail of Planet X: The SPHEREx Sky in Motion” is a public, interactive, Spanish-language website for exploring the infrared sky observed by NASA’s SPHEREx mission. When users arrive, a narrated voice introduces the mission. Users then navigate a sky map, dragging to rotate it and zooming in. They select a star and move a time slider to see where it was or will be, up to 20,000 years in the past or future. This makes stellar proper motion visible, using the same principle astronomers use to discover nearby objects: comparing positions on different dates. The site also includes:

a 3D mission globe;

a gallery of official SPHEREx images;

fact cards on celestial objects;

a space assistant that answers questions;

a section on the Planet X hypothesis, with a simulated 3D orbit.

What are its benefits?

It is free and requires no registration. It works on computers and phones, is in Spanish, and includes voice narration. It brings exploration, scientific data and learning together in one place, and it clearly separates what is real from what is simulated.

What is the intended impact?

We aim to bring real NASA data to Spanish-speaking students and communities across Latin America, to have the site used in science classes, and to inspire scientific careers and participation in citizen science. As next steps, we plan two improvements: letting users enter sky coordinates, and comparing real SPHEREx images taken on different dates to search for moving objects.

What tools did we use?

Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

Hardware: desktop computers for design and programming, and phones for mobile testing.

Hosting: Netlify.

Artificial intelligence: ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude.

Presentation and video: Canva and CapCut.

Data: NASA/JPL-Caltech, the IRSA archive and Aladin (CDS).

How is it creative?

The time slider turns thousands of years into seconds and reveals something the human eye cannot see: the motion of the stars. The site also combines interactive exploration, 3D graphics, voice narration and an assistant, and it connects the history of astronomy (from Neptune and Pluto to Planet Nine) with data from a mission launched in 2025.

What factors did we consider?

Accessibility: no registration, mobile-friendly and in Spanish.

Scientific validity: we used official sources and clearly labeled the simulations.

Ease of use: designed for people who are not experts.

Artificial intelligence: we used it responsibly and verified everything it produced.

Licensing: we respected usage permissions and credited the images.
